ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
Two cars, A and B, are moving in the same direction at constant velocities on a straight, level road, with car A trailing car B. At a certain moment when the distance between the two cars is $35\mathrm{m}$, car B, which is in front, suddenly brakes and decelerates. Taking this moment as the starting point of time, the velocity-time (v-t) diagrams of the motions of cars A and B are shown in the figure.

1. Determine the maximum separation between car A and car B.
2. If car A does not apply brakes, calculate the time duration after which a rear-end collision may occur.

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The figure is a velocity-time graph, with the vertical axis marked v/(m·s⁻¹) and the horizontal axis marked t/s. The graph line of car A is a horizontal line, with velocity constantly 4 m/s. The graph line of car B is a downward-sloping straight line, uniformly decelerating from 10 m/s at t=0 to 0 m/s at t=5 s; it intersects the horizontal line of car A at v=4 m/s, corresponding to time t=3 s. Reasoning: Initially car A is behind and car B is in front, and the distance between the two cars is 35 m. From 0 to 3 s, the velocity of car B is greater than the velocity of car A, and the distance increases; the amount of increase equals the area between the two v-t graph lines, namely the triangular area: 1/2 × 3 × (10−4)=9 m. Therefore the maximum distance is 35+9=44 m. From 3 to 5 s, the velocity of car A is greater than the velocity of car B, and A begins to catch up with B; the catching-up distance is the triangular area between the two velocity graph lines: 1/2 × 2 × 4=4 m. So at t=5 s, the distance between the two cars is 44−4=40 m. After 5 s, car B has stopped; if car A does not brake, it still moves forward at 4 m/s, and the time needed to catch up is 40/4=10 s. Therefore the total time from the start of timing to rear-end collision is 5+10=15 s.
